title: Websites & service portals
description: Help residents find a service, understand what they need and finish the task on a phone.
keywords: Websites & service portals Return to top Working example Open demo Help residents find a service, understand what they need and finish the task on a phone. Someone applying for a permit may have to piece together a department page, a PDF and a conversation by phone. Start by putting the instructions in one place. A permit applicant needs the service name, eligibility requirements and documents to bring. A staff editor needs one place to keep those details current. Try the service finder demonstration . Search by permit, roads, parks or records. Open a result to see the information a resident should prepare. Before moving pages, list the terms residents use when they telephone the department. Those terms belong in the new search index. Choose a published page that changes frequently. Ask the person who maintains it to show how a correction reaches the public site. Keep links to the current application and its supporting documents with the service instructions. 1. Service design Map resident questions to plain-language pages. Test the navigation against tasks such as renewing a license or requesting a record. Repeat the search with the words someone would use at the counter. 2. Content migration Inventory pages and documents, assign owners, map redirects and rehearse the cutover on a staging site. Check a saved address from the former site and confirm that it opens the corresponding service. 3. Editorial handover Give editors reusable page patterns and a publishing checklist. Walk an editor through a change before launch. Have a second editor find and correct the same instruction using the handover notes. 4. Scope and acceptance Ask a first-time visitor to locate the right service, check eligibility and open the application using only a keyboard. Ask an editor to update that same page. To estimate the work, count pages and documents, identify required languages and check the current CMS. Include integrations, editor permissions and the launch date. title: Data systems & reporting
description: Give staff a map or dashboard backed by a reporting pipeline they can check against source records.
keywords: Data systems & reporting Return to top Working example Open demo Give staff a map or dashboard backed by a reporting pipeline they can check against source records. When monthly totals differ between reports, staff need a way to trace the difference. Build the reconciliation step into the reporting process so staff can tell which records changed. Choose one number that staff already report. Trace it to the records, filters and calculation behind it. Try the service ledger demonstration . Select a district to compare its service records and hours. The CSV download follows the active district filter. Record how to treat a missing value, a correction and a row that was already present in the last refresh. Keep a small sample with known totals. A maintainer can run it again after a source field or reporting rule changes. For a map, preserve an identifier that lets a reviewer go from a point on the screen to the underlying record. 1. Source inventory Document the owner, format, refresh interval and allowed use of each source. Agree on a definition for each measure. Note when the source was last refreshed and which reporting period it covers. 2. Data preparation Validate incoming records, isolate exceptions and keep stable identifiers across refreshes. Include sample duplicates and missing values when checking the import. 3. Maps and reporting Design filters around decisions, include documented calculations and export the selected records. For an AI-assisted task, test its answers against a labeled sample before release. Open the export and reproduce the total using only its rows. 4. Scope and acceptance Filter a known sample, compare the count and sum to an independent calculation, then export the records and reproduce both numbers. Source quality, update frequency, geographic coverage, access rules and the number of reporting views drive effort. Open the planning guide · Scope and pricing

title: Mapping Indonesia’s industrial parks
description: How Rishabh Sinha built a public map and a repeatable publishing process for the University of Maryland’s Center for Global Sustainability.
keywords: Founder case study A public map of 141 industrial parks in Indonesia, built at the University of Maryland. Center for Global Sustainability Mapping Indonesia’s industrial parks Overview The research team had a spreadsheet full of evidence about Indonesia’s industrial parks. Rishabh Sinha built the website that lets readers explore it, then gave the team a way to publish the next edition. Organization Center for Global Sustainability Role Research assistant · Website engineering Period Fall 2023 to spring 2025 Java at night, seen from the International Space Station. NASA, Expedition 56 . Explore the map Engineering Outcome Sources Project data · May 2025 One archipelago, 141 parks. Explore the status recorded for each park in the handover dataset. Filter by status Inspect a park Ridgefolio rendering of the CGS status file ↗ . Boundaries from Natural Earth ↗ . Nearby points overlap at this scale. From spreadsheet to public map An operating park might draw power from the national grid, from a captive coal plant or from both. Readers needed to switch from park status to electricity supply without losing their place on the map. When researchers corrected a record, the downloadable file needed to reflect the same change. Regional distribution by status, replotted from the archived dashboard. Original chart calculation . A map and a set of research charts Rishabh connected the ArcGIS web map to thematic GeoJSON files. A reader can select a park to inspect its electricity supply or look up the sources behind a reported dispute. He also implemented nine Plotly charts from CSV data, including regional status and electricity capacity by industry. April 2025 chart code ↗ Electricity sources in the parks data Number of parks with each source flag PLN grid 84 Provider unclear 37 Captive gas 22 Solar 22 Captive coal 19 Bioenergy 10 Hydropower 2 One park can appear in several rows. Recalculated from the archived September CSV ↗ using the original chart calculation ↗ . A repeatable update Rishabh wrote a Python script that groups the master CSV fields into seven geographic files. He updated the public CSV download to use the master file and connected the site to the team’s selected ArcGIS map. A maintainer could regenerate the files, update the hosted layers and check the published map against the download. Generation script ↗ · Download and map changes ↗ Corrections after launch The team added Indonesia Huabao Industrial Park and updated the public methodology in October 2024. Rishabh added a contribution page with English and Bahasa Indonesia forms. His handover work with Molly Schreier covered replacing a map layer while preserving its colors and symbols. CGS methodology ↗ · Contribution page ↗ Launch, usage and research reuse 4,284 Recorded ArcGIS map-item views As of November 26, 2026, for the map connected in the May 2025 handover. Esri counts openings of the item page or viewer, including repeat visits. Public counter ↗ · How Esri counts views ↗ June 2024 Public launch CGS presented a downloadable dataset of 140 parks with six map layers . The launch deck shows the interface and how to read each layer. Launch presentation ↗ May 2025 Engineering handover The archived master table contains 141 named parks . Each of the seven geographic files contains the same 141 parks, with fields selected for its topic. Inspect the files ↗ December 2025 Research reuse CGS’s subsequent study of 106 nickel smelters lists the industrial parks dataset among the sources used to identify a smelter’s industrial park. This documents reuse of the team’s data. Methods, Appendix II ↗ Project records Rishabh built the website as a University of Maryland research assistant, working with Molly Schreier and Jiehong Lou. CGS and its collaborators collected and validated the data. The archived site credits the research team and the website creator separately. title: Evaluating an AI system
description: Rishabh authored a study on measuring whether a monitor can distinguish exposure to an instruction from a subsequent action.
keywords: AI monitor evaluation Research paper Return to top AI monitor evaluation Read paper Testing what an AI monitor can tell Rishabh authored a study on measuring whether a monitor can distinguish exposure to an instruction from a subsequent action. Read the paper and methods What the comparison found On the primary Qwen experiment, the monitor scored 0.853 AUROC and a trained text baseline scored 0.855. The paper shows how changing which examples enter the test changes what that score tells a reviewer. The study compares evaluation populations, reports results across models and includes a text baseline. The public paper links the experiment code. Relevance to a project For a buyer testing an assistant, the choice of examples matters. Evaluate correct answers, plausible errors and cases that should go to a human as separate groups.
